claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature plastic strain than commercially used pure tungsten.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature toughness than commercially used pure tungsten.
Atomic-size mismatches among W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr produce pronounced local lattice distortions and stress fields.
The heterogeneous strain fields created by lattice distortion act as distributed obstacles to dislocation motion at lower stresses.
Obstruction of dislocation motion by lattice-distortion fields improves the alloy's strength.
At high temperature, lattice-distortion-related obstacles promote dynamic recovery and dislocation rearrangement.
The proposed dynamic recovery and dislocation rearrangement increase plastic deformation capacity relative to pure tungsten.
The proposed dynamic recovery and dislocation rearrangement increase toughness relative to pure tungsten.
Pure tungsten has a more uniform lattice than equimolar WTaTiVZr.
The comparison should use pure tungsten and equimolar WTaTiVZr specimens with comparable grain sizes and microstructural features.
The WTaTiVZr comparison material is intended to have a homogeneous, precipitate-free microstructure with equiaxed grains.
Testing in an inert or vacuum atmosphere is intended to avoid oxidation effects.
Strain to failure is an appropriate measured indicator of plastic deformation capacity.
The area under the stress-strain curve is used as the measure of toughness.
TEM and XRD analyses can quantify or characterize local lattice distortion and dislocation behavior in the tested materials.
Residual processing defects or secondary-phase formation may affect the magnitude of the plastic-strain and toughness improvements.
